newsitem.title: UK: UK's fraudbusting chief says system fragmented.
newsitem.headline: UK's fraudbusting chief says system fragmented.

text.p: Britain's new "super" financial watchdog will partly unify the fight against fraud but the prosecution of such crimes remains fragmented, the head of Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said on Monday.

"There are still several distinct and different organisations all of which are concerned either with the prosecution or the regulation of fraud," SFO Director Rosalind Wright told Reuters after the release of the SFO's annual report.
While she welcomed the Labour government's plans to create a single financial watchdog, merging the separate "frontline regulators", it leaves open "the diversity in the criminal prosecution areas".
Wright, who last April became the fourth director of the SFO, said the current system was fragmented and inefficient. The SFO was created in 1988 to investigate major and complex fraud in Britain.

But the new unified regulatory structure would make it much easier for the SFO to have a dialogue with the regulators. "We'll be able to pass information over and they will be able to give us information much more readily than happens at the moment," she said.
The SFO report said it is probing 42 suspected frauds against investors, up from 29 a year ago.

Wright said she was concerned by the rise, which she put down to relative economic buoyancy and the billions of pounds of cash put in investors' pockets by the windfalls from converting building societies.

Among her suggestions for improving the prosecution and investigation of fraud, Wright believes judges could use regulatory powers to intervene early in an investigation by closing or suspending a firm to protect the public.
She said there was a good deal of support and enthusiasm for creating a single offence of "fraud". The Law Commission was giving it very close consideration and the SFO had made representations.
"We are hoping that they will be able to move that forward and produce draft legislation," she said.
Wright said criticism of the SFO's record was not warranted. "In eight cases out of 10 we get a conviction of at least one defendant in each case, usually the major defendant," she added.
The SFO director also raised the possibility of complicated and long fraud trials being tried by a panel rather than a jury.

The previous Conservative government was going to review the role of juries and the Labour government would "want to revisit this area and look at alternative ways of dealing with a tribunal for serious and complex fraud cases", she said.
Wright said her experience at City watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), which uses a tribunal for disciplinary offences, showed how trials could be simplified and shortened.
"They understand the nature of these transactions, something that is very difficult to explain to a lay jury," she said.

The SFO's new director also called for criminals to be hit "in the pocket where it hurts most" by imposing adequate fines along with custodial sentences. "We'd also like to see proper compensation paid to the victims of fraud," she said.
"At the end of the day what people who have been defrauded really want is not only the fraudster's head on a plate but they their money back as far as possible," she said.
